transcript.text: Dr. Morgan, here's my clinical staffing assessment. Two pediatric RNs and one RT for six simultaneous monitored-observation pediatric respiratory patients is not a ratio I can endorse as safe. Monitored respiratory observation patients can deteriorate quickly, and each may need aerosolized treatments, continuous monitoring checks, suctioning, and rapid escalation. With two RNs, you're looking at a 1:3 nurse-to-patient ratio for monitored respiratory patients, and a single RT covering six patients who may all need respiratory interventions simultaneously is a significant safety risk. If even one patient decompensates, the RT is occupied and the remaining patients are without dedicated respiratory coverage. My recommendation is that we can safely staff five monitored-observation bays with two RNs and one RT. At five patients, the ratio is more manageable -- 1:2.5 nursing coverage and one RT can reasonably attend to five patients if deterioration is caught early. This gives us a small but critical safety buffer. Luis, your point about designating one of the six oxygen-equipped bays as unavailable to hold us at five makes sense from both a facilities and staffing perspective. I'd rather plan for five staffed bays and have a clear escalation pathway for a sixth patient than commit to six with inadequate staffing and no margin.
